1:
Chrysostom marks the turn: having finished spiritual gifts the apostle passes to what is of all most necessary, and uses great earnestness, for the discourse is henceforth not of morals, not of one man's being a fornicator and another covetous, but about the very sum of all good things; as when a fever lays hold of the solid parts the mischief becomes incurable without much attention, so here it was reaching the very elements of godliness. Barnes calls this the most important portion of the letter, a connected and unanswerable argument for the main truth of Christianity, and more interesting to us as mortal beings with an instinctive dread of death than anything else in it. Tertullian, turning back to the subject, says he has defended it elsewhere against heretics of all sorts, but will not be wanting here either, for those ignorant of that little treatise.

What exactly was denied is disputed. Henry allows two possibilities, that they turned the doctrine into allegory, as Hymeneus and Philetus did by saying it was already past, or that they rejected it as absurd on principles of reason; he concludes they denied it in the proper sense and so disowned a future state of recompences, which is not strange in infidels though surprising in Christians who had their religion by revelation. Ellicott reports the suggestion that the apostle combats a false conception rather than a denial, the resurrection being refined away into a rising from the death of sin into a life of righteousness; but he judges from the emphatic later statement and the drift of the argument that a denial is meant. Calvin says it is uncertain whether they doubted only the resurrection of the body or the immortality of the soul too: some philosophers held souls immortal, but the resurrection of the body never entered the mind of any of them, while the Sadducees had grosser views and thought the soul a breath of wind without substance.

Gill observes that the doctrine of the resurrection is here called the Gospel, being a fundamental article of it, and that the raising of Christ made a considerable part in the apostles' ministry, to the grief of the Sadducees, the scorn of the Gentile philosophers, and the comfort of the faithful. Robertson notes that the opening verb is almost a reproach, that the gospel is a cognate accusative, the gospel which he gospelized to them, and that the relatives run on without a connecting word. Clarke sets out the chapter's three questions: whether there be a resurrection of the dead, what the nature of the risen bodies will be, and what use we should make of the doctrine.

The two conditions are read with care. Clarke takes the first to mean that they are now in a salvable state, saved from their heathenism and former sins, their being brought finally to glory depending on faithfulness to the grace received. Barnes names that reading and refuses it: the words mean not merely that they were brought into a salvable state, but that their hopes of eternal life rested on this and that by it they were in fact saved from sin's condemnation. Wesley holds a middle course: salvation is begun and will be perfected if they continue in the faith. Ellicott renders the second clause as holding fast with what word the gospel was preached, and says the sense is not that they were converted and no results followed, but that faith saves them unless the whole gospel be false. Robertson makes both conditions of the first class, so that the apostle assumes they hold it fast while holding the peril over them in their temptation to deny the resurrection. Calvin calls the two expressions very cutting, since so sudden a fall proved that they had never understood what was delivered to them, or that their knowledge had been loose and floating.
3:
The opening phrase is taken of rank, not sequence. Gill says it means not only first in order but among the chief and principal things, and Robertson that it refers not to time but to importance. On the receiving, Robertson notes that direct revelation is claimed in the same terms used of the institution of the Supper, with the same pair of verbs. Clarke says it was by revelations from God himself and not from man; Barnes counts this a claim to divine guidance; Wesley that it came from Christ himself and was no fiction of his own. Ellicott says the verse shows the subject of apostolic teaching, not all the gospel taught but what was put in the forefront as of first importance, the historical fact of the death, the burial and the rising, and calls this the first creed of Christendom. Robertson reports the same from Stanley and qualifies it with Vincent, that it is rather a sample of the apostle's early teaching than a profession of faith by converts, and counts four items carried by four verbs: he died, was buried, has been raised, appeared.

On the clause about our sins they agree. Barnes says he died as an expiatory offering on their account, and calls the passage full proof that he did not die merely as a martyr. Clarke calls the death a vicarious sacrifice essential to the gospel scheme of salvation. Ellicott says the phrase means not only because of but in behalf of our sins, to take them away, and that the atonement was not evolved out of the apostle's own consciousness but revealed to him. Robertson glosses the preposition as over, in behalf of, and even instead of. Calvin observes that the resurrection is confirmed here as a fundamental doctrine of the gospel, laid as a foundation in the erecting of a house, and that the authority of the preaching is heightened by his bringing forward nothing but what had been enjoined on him, delivered as from hand to hand.

The burial is not passed over. Ellicott says it is dwelt upon as proof of the reality of the death, as the entombment of Lazarus shows that he rose from death and not a trance. Gill collects the prophecies, that he should make his grave with the wicked and with the rich, fulfilled through the rich man of Arimathea who begged the body and laid it in his own new tomb.

The repeated appeal to the Scriptures draws most comment. Ellicott says the reiteration shows how strongly the apostle dwelt on the unity of the facts with the predictions of the prophets, the Gospel narratives not yet being in existence, so that the rising was no later invention. Clarke concedes that it is nowhere said in express terms that Christ should rise on the third day, but holds it implied in the types, in the prophet delivered from the fish and particularly in Isaac, whose being brought bound to the mount pointed to the death as his being brought back pointed to the rising. Barnes concedes the same, that what was foretold was the rising and not necessarily its day, and refers the proof to the psalm. Robertson notes that the verb for the raising is a perfect and not an aorist, the change being deliberate, since the apostle wishes to emphasise its permanence: he is still risen. Wesley observes that the proof is drawn first from Scripture and then from a cloud of witnesses. Cyril of Jerusalem, taking the apostle to have sent us back to the testimonies, proposes to verify the proofs of the rising as those of the cross were verified, learning from the Scriptures its season and place and whether the women who sought and found him not afterwards rejoiced, so that the Gospel narratives may not be thought fables.
5:
Barnes states the method: the resurrection was a fact to be proved, like all facts, by competent witnesses, and the apostle appeals to those who yet lived to attest it, so many not possibly having been deceived. Calvin says he brings forward eyewitnesses, though not all, since he omits the women. Gill notices the same omission: Peter was not the first by whom Christ was seen, since he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, but the women's testimony is passed over and Peter seems the first of the men. Robertson insists the verb means not a mere vision but an actual appearance, and notes that this appearance to Peter, mentioned here incidentally, elsewhere determines the joyful faith of the disciples.

The name of the group raises a difficulty, since after Judas died only eleven remained. Clarke reports that several authorities read eleven, supported by one Gospel, but suggests twelve points out the society of the apostles, who though then eleven kept their original number as a name. Wesley says the same in a line, that it was their standing appellation though the full number was absent. Ellicott makes it a corporate title, as a council is named without regard to how many attend, and Calvin, raising the arithmetic directly, reports an older opinion that the appearance followed the choosing of Matthias.

The larger company is the strongest testimony. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley place it probably in Galilee, where most disciples had been made, and Barnes remarks that every evangelist omits it. Clarke calls it remarkable, since most of the five hundred were alive when the apostle wrote, so that he might have been confronted had he dared assert a falsity; Robertson dates the letter within twenty-five years and identifies the occasion with the meeting on the mountain. Ellicott notes that the word for those who had died is the one used of Stephen. On the next witness Gill argues that it cannot be the son of Zebedee, killed by Herod years before, but the son of Alphaeus, still living and of great credit with the Jews; Robertson calls him the brother of the Lord and finds here why the brothers of Jesus were in the upper room. Barnes observes that no evangelist records it, and Wesley takes the next title to reach beyond the twelve to the seventy.

His own case is handled with most care. Barnes says the passage proves he saw the same Lord and the same body the others had seen, or his assertion would be no proof; it was not fancy, nor imagination, nor even a revelation that Christ had risen, but a real sight of the ascended Redeemer. Gill agrees that it was a sight of Christ in heaven and not on earth, such as Stephen had, and corporeal, or it would have been beside the point here. Calvin says that being no deceptive vision it was fit to establish belief in the resurrection. Clarke observes that it seems to have been essential to a primitive apostle to have seen and conversed with Christ, and that Jesus appears never to have shown himself to anyone after this. Robertson gives the literal sense of the strange word as a miscarriage, first found in Aristotle and used in the Greek version and the papyri. Lightfoot traces it further: the Greek translators render the untimely birth of Job by it, and render a hidden untimely birth as one proceeding out of the womb, though the Hebrew denotes the contrary, that it never went out; the Chaldee has it hidden in the womb, and the term is usual among the Talmudists. Ellicott renders the clause that he appeared last of all as to an untimely born one, and Wesley says it was impossible to abase himself more: as an abortion is not worthy the name of a man, so he calls himself not worthy the name of an apostle.
9:
Gill says the title refers not to his stature but to the figure just used, and expresses not the opinion of others but his own true sense of himself. Barnes locates the reason: not any defect in his commission or want of qualification to witness what he saw, but the great crime of his life, that he had been a persecutor, which he could never forget. Robertson notes that the word is a true superlative, compares the places where he calls himself less than the least of all saints and chief of sinners, and observes that under attack from the Judaizers he still claimed rank equal to any apostle. Wesley draws the lesson that believers are humbled all their lives, even for sins committed before they believed. Clarke resolves the apparent contradiction by a distinction: as a man and a minister he was greater than any of the twelve, but as an apostle less, because not originally of that body, and none of the twelve had persecuted Christ.

Calvin asks whether the confession was forced from him: it is not certain whether his enemies threw this out to detract from his credit or whether it was of his own accord, and though the apostle was always cheerfully disposed to abase himself that he might magnify grace, he suspects that here he wished to obviate calumnies. Ellicott treats it as a digression into which the memory of his conversion led him, in which his own inherent nothingness and his greatness by grace are mingled in expressions of intense personal feeling. Cyril of Jerusalem turns the fact into an argument, professing wonder that the Spirit confined the letters of the rest to a small number but gave the former persecutor the privilege of writing fourteen, not because Peter or John was less, but that the doctrine might be beyond question.

On the grace and the labour the readings divide. Clarke says he was not unfaithful to the call but used the grace given him, and that his labours, travels and sufferings prove he wrought more than the whole twelve. Wesley makes the labour spring from a deep sense of the peculiar love God had shown him, adding that it was not he but the grace of God which qualified him and still excites him to diligence. Calvin names and refuses the inference drawn here, that God offers grace while the right use of it remains in a man's own power; the words give it no support, since nothing is claimed as the apostle's own. Barnes observes that nothing is more common in these writings than the tracing of everything to God's mere mercy, and nothing a more certain mark of true piety. Gill says he was what he was, privately and as a minister, purely by grace. Robertson notes that the relative is neuter, naming what he was rather than who. Ellicott finds the verse full of that official dignity joined with personal humility characteristic of the man.

Chrysostom describes the manoeuvre whole: having exalted the Apostles and abased himself, then exalted himself above them so as to make out an equality and prove himself worthy of credit, he does not dismiss them but ranks himself with them again, pointing out their concord in Christ, yet not as one tacked on but as appearing in the same rank, for so it was profitable for the Gospel. Barnes says it is immaterial by whom the truth was established, and Ellicott that the words recall the reader from the digression to the main argument. Calvin notes that the verb for preaching is present, intimating perseverance in teaching the same thing, and that otherwise their apostleship would be void and the readers' religion go for nothing. Clarke adds that whoever teaches contrary does not preach the apostolic doctrine, the primitive apostles being those who had seen Christ and had their call immediately from him.
12:
Barnes describes the turn: having stated the direct evidence for the rising of the Lord, the apostle now shows that the dead will rise by drawing it from that fact and by drawing the consequences of denial, the whole argument resting on the one event. Calvin says a reciprocal inference holds good both ways and both affirmatively and negatively, since Christ did not die or rise for himself but for us, so that his resurrection is the foundation and substance of ours, and what was accomplished in him must be fulfilled in us. Ellicott puts it as logic: a man has been proved by historical fact to have risen from the dead, so it is illogical to say that there is no resurrection of the dead. Robertson says the question springs naturally from the proof just given, and that the answer to the sceptics is simply the fact, since it all turns on this.

Who the deniers were is guessed at differently. Henry says some among them thought the resurrection an impossibility, a common sentiment among the heathens, and that the apostle answers with an incontestable fact and then argues from the absurdities their principle entails. Wesley supposes in a line that they had probably been heathen philosophers. Clarke suspects a false teacher endeavouring to incorporate Mosaic rites with Christian doctrine and even to blend Sadducean opinions with the whole, and says the chapter was written to confute this mongrel Christian. Robertson calls them sceptics at Corinth, possibly within the church, denying that dead people rise as some now deny that miracles happen.

The counter-argument is then run backwards, and its fairness is noticed. Barnes says the same difficulties stand in the way of raising him as in any other case: he was dead and buried, had lain three days, the soul had left the body, the frame was cold and stiff, the blood had ceased to circulate and the lungs to heave; if it is impossible that the dead should rise, he has not been raised. Clarke observes that some at Corinth seem to have denied the resurrection of the dead yet admitted that Christ had risen, and answers that if he was raised mankind may be, and if mankind cannot be then his body never was. Gill takes the denial at its widest, that no such thing is possible or ever was or will be true in fact, and Wesley calls it flatly impossible. Robertson says the argument is turned round with tremendous force, and adds that it is fair.

The consequences follow one by one. Barnes says the word for vain includes useless, idle and false, since it would be false to affirm the system was from heaven and useless to proclaim one that could save no one. Clarke says the doctrine would be nugatory and belief of it unprofitable. Robertson glosses the word as empty, and says that if the sceptics refuse the fact they have nothing to stand on. Ellicott traces the chain: the apostles had preached a risen Christ and their converts believed in one, so that if there is no resurrection he is not risen and preaching and faith alike rest on a delusion; the argument, he insists, stays an appeal to historical evidence and to the consequences of denying it. Calvin presses the word furthest, that the preaching would be empty not merely as having some mixture of falsehood but as an entire fallacy: what remains if Christ has been swallowed up by death, become extinct, been overwhelmed by the curse of sin and overcome by Satan? Where that article is subverted all the rest is of no moment, and there can be no solidity of faith where no hope of life is seen, since in the death considered apart from the rising nothing appears but ground of despair. Wesley notes that the commission itself was given after the resurrection.
15:
The next absurdity touches the witnesses. Gill says the apostles were chosen for this office and sent into all the world to testify, so that if Christ is not risen they have borne a false witness, than which no more odious character can be fixed on a man. Ellicott sharpens it: they would be not mistaken witnesses but men testifying to what they knew to be false, not deceived but deceivers; the suppressed premise is that they had no motive to lie. Clarke presses it practically, asking whether five hundred could agree in such an imposition, and whether, if they did, some one would not have discovered the cheat, having much to gain by revealing it; such a case never occurred and never can. Robertson notes that the genitive may be read of God's service or as concerning God, though with the following preposition the natural sense is against God. Calvin counts it no trivial absurdity either, that men ordained to be heralds of eternal truth should be detected as deceivers of the world, which tends to God's highest dishonour.

The argument is then stated over again. Gill says the repetition shows the importance of the point and brings out further absurdities, and Barnes that the truth is great and momentous enough to bear repeating. Ellicott marks a change of method, the historical argument being complete and the apostle turning to a reduction to absurdity.

The first new absurdity is that they remain unforgiven. Barnes says their faith would be vain because they would still be unpardoned sinners, pardon being bound up with belief in the rising. Robertson observes that the word for vain here is stronger than the one used before, meaning devoid of truth, and that the death has no atoning value if he did not rise, since he was then only a man like other men. Clarke reasons from the other end: if Christ has not risen there is no proof that he was not justly put to death, since God would not raise a malefactor, and then he has made no atonement. Wesley says more than the reformation plainly wrought in them was needed, even the atonement whose sufficiency God attested by raising our great Surety from the grave. Calvin grants everything the death accomplished, the atoning for sins, the crucifying of the old man, the destroying of death and of the devil, and then withdraws it all: none of it would have stood had he not by rising come off victorious, so that if the resurrection is overthrown the dominion of sin returns.

The second reaches the dead and the third the living. Gill reports that some take those fallen asleep of martyrs only, but holds all believers meant. Clarke says their bodies are dissolved in the earth despite the promise to raise them, their hope without foundation. Barnes says all Christians who had died would have failed of salvation, Wesley that they have lost their life and being together, and Calvin asks what advantage it were to the dead that they once were Christians. On the last verse the readings differ. Barnes reports that some refer it to the apostles only. Clarke would repunctuate it to read that if in this life we have hoped in Christ only we are more to be pitied than all men, and Robertson makes the word only govern the whole clause, adding that a hope limited to this life leaves nothing beyond, so that the Epicureans have the argument on us. Calvin goes furthest, that we should not merely lose our time and pains but that it were better not to believe at all, the condition of unbelievers being preferable. Wesley turns it round: if we have a hope full of immortality and taste the powers of the world to come, then despite all present trials we are happier than all men.
20:
Barnes hears the change of tone: the language is the bursting forth of a full heart and overpowering conviction, as if the apostle were impatient of slow argument and longing to utter what he knew, having seen the risen Lord. Ellicott says he turns from the ghastly conclusion of the hypothesis to the hopeful faith belief in the resurrection brings. Robertson calls the verse the logical triumph after the reduction to absurdity. Gill says the fact is reassumed from the contradictions that follow its denial, and Calvin that after showing what confusion would follow the apostle again assumes it as certain.

The figure of the firstfruits is worked out from the calendar. Lightfoot says that although the rising harmonises with firstfruits of any kind, it agrees especially with the offering of the sheaf, in the thing itself and in the circumstance of time: first came the Passover, the day following was a sabbatic day, and on the day after that the firstfruits were offered; so Christ our passover was sacrificed, the day following was the sabbath, and on the day after that he rose. Clarke takes it up, remarking that the Judaizing teacher at Corinth would feel its force sooner than we can, and that as surely as firstfruits prove a harvest, so surely does this prove ours. Ellicott adds that if the letter was written near Passover that sequence may have suggested the image, and insists that Christ rose to the inclusion and not the exclusion of humanity. Henry presses the same from the law of the offering: the whole lump was made holy by the consecration of the firstfruits, so that the rising is as much an earnest that the dead in him shall rise as that the harvest should be accepted. Wesley calls it the earnest and pledge of their resurrection who slept in him. Robertson observes that others raised from the dead died again, but not Jesus, and that the word for sleeping gives us our cemetery.

The two men are then set against each other. Calvin says the point is that Christ was not raised merely as an individual, and proves it from contraries, since death is not from nature but from man's sin: as Adam did not die for himself alone but for us all, so Christ, the antitype, did not rise for himself alone, having come to restore all that was ruined; the argument runs not by similitude or example but by something stronger. Gill explains that all men were in Adam seminally, as the common parent of human nature, and representatively, he being the federal head and a type of Christ to come. Barnes draws the consequence that death would not have entered but for transgression, man having otherwise remained immortal or been translated without seeing death, as Enoch and Elijah were. Clarke states it in a line, mortality by Adam and immortality by Christ. Robertson names him the Second Adam. Ellicott says the firstfruit must be a sample of the same kind as what it represents, and that the two stand as heads of humanity, Christ's federal relation to mankind not being dated from the incarnation.

How far the second all reaches is disputed. Robertson admits the thought is not easy to catch, holds that the verb means restoration to life and not necessarily salvation, and allows that the two companies may not coincide. Wesley limits it expressly to the righteous, and observes that the apostle does not say they shall revive, as naturally as they die, but be made alive by a power not their own. Barnes guards the first clause: men did not become actually dead when Adam sinned, having then no existence, but their death is traced to him as procuring cause. Ellicott divides the inheritance instead: what is fleshly in us comes from the one, what is spiritual from the other.
23:
The word for order is military. Barnes says it relates to a cohort marshalled with the officers at the head and every man in his place, and Robertson to each man's own division. Gill rules out the wrong senses: not of time, nor dignity, nor age, nor condition. Clarke and Ellicott count three groups, Christ, then those who are his at his coming, then the end; Clarke will not assert this is exactly the intended order, and Ellicott notes that the interval between the last two is not described. Robertson adds that the word for the coming was the technical term for a royal visit, with advent-coins struck afterwards. Calvin treats it as anticipating an objection: if the life of Christ draws ours along, why do we lie rotting while he has risen? God has appointed another order. Wesley notes that the wicked rise at the same time but are not taken into the account here.

On the end and the surrender they turn on what kingdom is meant. Barnes says it denotes the completion of the work of redemption, the winding up of affairs under the mediatorial reign. Clarke defines that reign as comprehending all the displays of grace in saving sinners and all spiritual influence in governing the Church, and takes the rule abolished to include earthly governments. Ellicott extends it to all intermediate rule, good and bad, since God is at last to govern all creatures directly, and humanity, having shared the condition of fallen Adam, will be restored to that of unfallen Adam. Wesley guards the point that the Father does not then begin to reign without the Son, nor the Son cease to reign, the divine reign of both being from everlasting, so that only the mediatorial kingdom is meant. Robertson observes that the construction is indefinite as to time.

Why he must reign is variously grounded. Wesley says because so it is written, and Clarke rests it on the promise, adding that the kingdom cannot be given up till all rule is cast down, so that while the world lasts all men are his subjects. Ellicott reverses that: some suggest he must reign because it was prophesied, but the more obvious truth is that it was prophesied because it is morally necessary, since God must triumph. Barnes takes the word of propriety and of what was predicted of him. Calvin says the Father placed him at his right hand on the understanding that he should not resign that authority until his enemies were subdued, which is said to console the pious against impatience at the delay. Cyril of Jerusalem answers those who read the words the other way and say that when his enemies are put under his feet he shall cease to reign: he who is king before he has subdued them, how shall he not the rather be king after gaining the mastery?

The last enemy is then defined. Gill says it is not eternal death, since the wicked remain under that, but a corporeal death, an enemy as the wages of sin and the curse of the law, contrary to human nature and destructive of the work of God's hands. Clarke says the verb means to be counter-worked, subverted and finally overturned, and argues that death cannot be destroyed by there being simply no further death, but only by a general resurrection; so the promise assures that resurrection and proves that after it there shall be no more death. Barnes places the other foes earlier, the enmity of the heart subdued by the gospel, the sceptre of Satan wrested from him and the false religions destroyed, so that nothing remains but death, overcome by the rising. Wesley arranges them by history: Satan brought in sin and sin brought forth death, and Christ conquered them in that order, Satan, then sin in his death, then death in his resurrection.
27:
The quotation is unnamed and its application disputed. Barnes says the apostle refers to a prediction without quoting one, that the words stand in a psalm as applicable to man, and that whether the psalm refers to the Messiah has been made a question. Calvin allows the same source but names two difficulties: the prophet speaks not of Christ alone but of the whole human race, and by all things means only what serves the convenience of bodily life. Gill answers that the man there cannot be Adam in innocence, since the word signifies a frail mortal man, which he then was not, nor could he be called a son of man. Ellicott makes the preceding verse a parenthesis, so the connecting word reaches back to the reign, and takes the psalm to say that God put all things under man and in a higher sense under the Son of Man. Clarke would parenthesise this one.

The exception is noticed by all. Clarke says it shows that the divine nature is not subjected to the human, since Christ as Messiah and Mediator must ever be inferior to the Father, and his human nature, however dignified by union with the divine, inferior to God. Robertson observes that either Christ or God may be supplied as subject, and that the perfect marks a state of completion. Cyril of Jerusalem presses the words the other way: the Lord says this to the Lord, not to a servant but to his own Son, and the Only-begotten is Lord of all yet the obedient Son, for he did not grasp the Lordship but received it by the Father's will, neither grasping it nor the Father grudging to impart it.

The subjection of the Son is handled carefully. Gill says all things are not yet put under him in fact, though in right the Father has given him power to dispose of them at his pleasure. Barnes reads the same, that the time has not arrived and the dominion is now being exercised as the plans move forward. Clarke fixes the moment: when the administration of the kingdom of grace is closed, and there is no state of probation and no need to distinguish grace from glory, then the Son, as man and Messiah, ceases to exercise any distinct dominion. Wesley says the same in a phrase, that he delivers up the mediatorial kingdom. Robertson notes that the aorist subjunctive has given translators needless trouble here, the sentence being prophecy. Cyril of Jerusalem again answers an inference, that some have dared to say the words show the Son shall be absorbed into the Father, and asks whether the creatures of Christ shall continue while Christ perishes, by whom they were made; and whether, if other things abide when subject to the Son, the Son should not abide when subject to the Father.

The closing phrase is taken as the end of everything. Ellicott says they express the complete redemption both of the race and of the individual, the sublime conclusion to which the moral enthusiasm and earnest logic of the argument has brought us. Wesley expands it, that all things and consequently all persons, without interruption, without the intervention of any creature and without the opposition of any enemy, shall be subordinate to God; even an inspired apostle can see nothing beyond it. Robertson calls it the final goal of all the redemptive plans of God. Calvin alone asks how far it reaches, whether it holds in the Devil and wicked men, and answers that it does not, unless the verb be taken otherwise; at present, while the Devil resists God and wicked men confound his order, it does not distinctly appear, but when Christ has executed judgment and cast down Satan and all the wicked, the glory of God will be conspicuous even in their destruction.
29:
They agree first on the difficulty. Clarke calls it the most difficult verse in the New Testament, there being nearly as many interpretations as interpreters. Barnes says there is perhaps no passage over which there has been greater variety, expositors not harmonizing even now. Robertson reports that Stanley lists thirteen interpretations and that over thirty have been suggested; the Greek expositors took the phrase to mean about the dead, baptism being itself a burial and a rising. Chrysostom offers to mention how the Marcionite heretics pervert it, knowing he will excite much laughter. Ellicott suggests the abruptness is less startling if the apostle paused for breath after the outburst just finished, or postponed the dictation to another day.

The readings offered are various. Lightfoot takes baptism here for martyrdom, a sense he finds in the Gospels, so the question is what those shall do who undergo martyrdom if there is no rising. Wesley offers two, that they were baptized in hope of blessings to be received after being numbered with the dead, or in the room of the dead, like soldiers advancing into the place of companions who fell before them. Gill lays out three possibilities: a Jewish washing, Christian baptism literally, or baptism as a figure. Calvin sets aside the common exposition, and holds that the baptism received by those already reckoned as dead is of no avail if there is no resurrection.

The second argument is drawn from their own danger. Ellicott points to the strong contrast between them in one verse and we in the next, and says the conduct of the apostles would be equally illogical on the same supposition. Barnes says such efforts would be vain and foolish unless a glorious resurrection awaited, since they had no other object. Robertson observes that he was never out of danger from Damascus to his last visit to Rome. Calvin restricts it to voluntary dangers, into which believers throw their lives for the confession of Christ, and says such magnanimity would be ascribed to rashness rather than firmness if the saints perished at death. Gill extends the reproach beyond the martyrs to ministers and private Christians who expose themselves continually, asking who in his senses would do so if the dead rise not. Wesley says plainly that no amends can be expected in this life.

The oath and the beasts close the passage. Barnes calls the opening word a particle of swearing and reports the manuscripts divided between our rejoicing and your; Robertson notes that there is no word for protest at all, the oath being carried by the particle. Ellicott says his converts are his boast, and that such a life, in its inward battles and ceaseless conflict with enemies, was indeed a daily dying. Lightfoot takes the boasting rather as the Corinthians' boasting against him, and Clarke, following him, says the apostle considered himself continually trampled on and exposed to contempt, but took it as part of the reproach of Christ. Wesley says love makes their rejoicing his own. On the beasts they divide sharply. Lightfoot holds them literal, that the apostle was really cast to wild beasts in the theatre, and answers the objection from silence by how much else the historian omitted. Clarke argues the other way from that same silence, the apostle's own when enumerating his sufferings and the historian's alike. Robertson allows that some take the verb literally, and that a place in the ruins of Ephesus is still called a prison of Paul, but objects that a Roman citizen could not lawfully be so used. Wesley takes it for a proverb of the most imminent danger, and Gill reports the figurative readings, that the beasts are Satan or men of savage disposition. Calvin corrects Erasmus, that those meant are not men thrown to the beasts but men condemned to fight them.
33:
The argument turns to exhortation. Barnes marks the change, that the apostle now entreats where he had been reasoning, and explains the danger: there was much plausible in the objections and much subtilty in the teachers who denied the doctrine, and perhaps something in the cast of their own minds, accustomed to abstruse inquiry rather than to simple facts. Ellicott says the preceding words were spoken with sarcasm, and that the solemn thought then occurs that they may describe too truly the state of some, tainted by the bad moral atmosphere they lived in. Gill names two sources of the deceit, those who deny the doctrine and reason about it, and the libertines who argue from the denial in favour of a licentious life. Calvin warns that nothing is easier than to glide into profane speculation under pretext of inquiry, and that such talk has more effect than we suppose in polluting our minds and corrupting our morals. Robertson and Wesley both take the deceit to lie in a false philosophy of life.

The saying quoted is traced. Clarke says there are many like it among the Greek poets, that this one makes an iambic verse and is supposed to come from a lost comedy of Menander, and sets beside it a rabbinic proverb of two dry logs and one green, where the dry burnt up the green. Ellicott agrees on the source, the line being modified in one word, and adds that we cannot say whether the apostle knew the poem. Robertson allows that it may equally have been a current proverb which he could have taken from either source. On the sense they are of one mind: Clarke says he who frequents the company of corrupt men will soon be as they are, Barnes explains the first word as a being together and close intercourse, Robertson the second as custom and morals, and Wesley says discourse contrary to faith, hope or love tends to destroy all holiness.

The call that follows is read as a summons out of drunkenness. Barnes says the verb denotes waking from a deep sleep or torpor and is usually applied to those who become sober after drunkenness. Calvin says the same, that it properly signifies to become sober, the Greek version using it so of drunkards. Robertson renders it simply to wake up as from drunkenness, and the following clause as an order to stop sinning. Gill represents them as inebriated with bad principles, fallen asleep and grown remiss in the exercise of grace. Wesley calls the word an exclamation full of apostolical majesty and adds that sin supposes drowsiness of soul. On the adverb they differ. Barnes offers two senses, rouse to the ways of righteousness or rouse as it is right that you should, and prefers the second. Clarke insists that the word should be rendered awake fully and thoroughly, as ye ought, and not awake to righteousness. Ellicott renders it awake to soberness in a righteous manner, and says the section and the direct proofs close with this call.

The reproach at the close is felt by all of them. Clarke says the original is very emphatic, that some have an ignorance of God, a sort of substantial darkness preventing the light from penetrating the soul, which is worse than simply being in the dark. Robertson names it agnosticism and remarks that some now take pride in it instead of shame. Wesley says that with all their boasted knowledge they are totally ignorant of what most concerns them, and that nothing is more shameful than a sleepy ignorance of God and of his word and works, considering the advantages they had enjoyed. Ellicott takes the shame to cover not only the last words but the whole preceding argument, since it was a shame that to Christians the apostle should have to vindicate the very fundamental truth of the faith.
35:
Barnes says the second part of the chapter opens here. Henry calls it a plausible and principal objection, and plainly twofold: by what means can they be raised, and what power is equal to such an effect? Wesley states it in the objector's terms, how the dead rise after their whole frame is dissolved, and with what bodies, after these are mouldered into dust. Robertson calls the apostle a master at putting the standpoint of the imaginary adversary, says this is still the great objection, and that we know the how of very few things. On the questioner they differ: Clarke thinks it the false apostle at Corinth, to whom the letter often refers covertly, while Gill allows it may be a weak believer among the babes in Christ. Calvin grants the force of the question, since nothing is more at variance with human reason than this article, and none but God could persuade us that bodies now liable to corruption, after rotting or burning or being torn by wild beasts, shall be restored entire and better.

The answer opens with a rebuke. Ellicott says the Greek does not carry the opprobrium of the word forbidden in the Gospel, and renders it senseless one: you who sow seed with your own hand ask such a question. Robertson calls it a severe term justified because the objector plumes himself on his acuteness, and remarks that sceptics pose as the intelligentsia though the pose does not make them intelligent. Clarke finds a peculiar propriety in it if the false apostle is addressed, and adds that it is folly to call a thing impossible because one cannot comprehend it. Lightfoot supplies the Jewish parallel, that the Talmudists used the same word, and that Rabban Jochanan ben Zakkai answered the Boethusians, who also denied the resurrection, by calling them fools. Chrysostom notices that the style here is pungent, against the apostle's usual gentleness, because of the impiety of the gainsayers.

The seed answers the question of manner. Calvin says the apostle might have replied that the mode incomprehensible to us is easy with God, and that we should assign to his secret power the honour of believing what we cannot comprehend; but he goes another way, showing that the resurrection is so far from being against nature that we see it daily illustrated. Wesley says the objection is thereby inverted, since death is so far from hindering life that it goes before it, and Barnes that the same difficulty lies against an everyday fact. Ellicott is careful about what this achieves: the apostle proves nothing here, since analogy can never prove, but shows a resurrection possible and substantial identity preserved under variation of form.

What is sown and what rises are then distinguished. Gill says the sower does not take a stalk in the blade and ear and sow that, and Barnes that one kernel is sown to produce many, so the body raised is not the same in the sense that the same particles compose it. Robertson makes the point sharply, that we sow seeds and not plants, and that the butterfly comes out of the dying worm; even under the microscope the germ plasm may seem almost identical while the plant is quite distinct. Clarke marvels at the increase, that out of one bare grain come a system of roots, a tall stalk with its leaves and the full corn in the ear, several hundred times what was deposited, and denies that nature can effect it. Gill insists that it is not the husbandman nor the sun nor the rain that gives the grain its form but God, who does not create that form but gives it to the selfsame grain. Wesley presses further, that the body given is not only peculiar to the species but proper to that individual, arising out of the substance of that very grain.
39:
The argument moves from plants to animals. Gill grants what is common to all flesh, that it agrees in its original, is supported by food and is alike frail, yet denies that it is of equal worth, the flesh of men being animated by a rational soul and set first. Clarke presses the difference to the senses, that no two kinds of animals have flesh of the same flavour; and against those who hold fish not to be flesh he answers that they might as well say a lily is not a vegetable. Ellicott states it the other way, that all organisms have the same basis and a structural unit runs through animal life, but God gives it a vast variety of form, so that the prescience which fits each kind to its condition can give another hereafter; had we seen flesh in one shape only and been told it could live in the sea, we might equally have asked with what body. Robertson observes that variety exists along with kinship, so that even if evolution proved true the argument would stand. Barnes concludes that since bodies already differ in qualities and forms it is not absurd for God to raise the human body with different properties. Calvin says the substance is the same while the quality differs, and that whatever diversity we see in any kind is a prelude of the resurrection, God showing that it is no difficult thing for him to renew our bodies by changing their condition.

The eye is then lifted from earth to heaven, though what is meant is disputed. Barnes takes the two classes plainly, the sun and moon and stars on one side and the bodies of men and brutes and insects on the other, and asks whether a difference between our present and future bodies can be strange when two such classes already exist. Wesley says the brightest lustre the earthly can reach is widely different from that of the heavenly. Clarke denies that the terms are used as we use them, since the apostle speaks of human beings, some clothed with celestial and some with terrestrial bodies, and takes the first for such refined bodies as those in which Enoch and Elijah and Christ appear in glory. Ellicott reports the view of many that the celestial bodies are those of angels, whose appearances on earth are accompanied by a blaze of light, but thinks it better to take the verse as a general statement expanded in the next. Robertson notes that the argument now rises above the merely terrestrial, and that experience raises no objection to a glory belonging to the spiritual body.

Within the heavens a further difference appears. Barnes marks the change of thought, that the previous verse set class against class while this finds the difference inside one class, the sun more splendid than the moon and the stars differing among themselves. Clarke follows the same descent, sun brighter than moon, moon than planets, planets than stars, and among the fixed stars one more splendid than another, whether from their magnitudes or the nearness of some to us we cannot tell. Robertson says the telescope has added force to the argument, since stars differ in magnitude and brilliancy. Gill calls the sun the greater light and the fountain of light. Ellicott draws the conclusion for the whole passage, that the God who is not limited to a monotonous form for physical nature need be in no difficulty about another form for human nature, and adds that the force of all three analogies is that identity of matter is preserved amid variety of form. Calvin warns against a mistake commonly made in applying this, since it is supposed the apostle meant that after the resurrection the saints will have different degrees of honour, which is not his point.
42:
The analogies are now applied. Ellicott says that as identity is preserved amid ever-varying form in plants, animals and inorganic matter, so a change in the form of our organism is compatible with personal identity, the it remaining the same. Barnes says the dead are raised as grain springs up, and Gill that the risen bodies will be the same in substance yet as different as the full corn in the ear from the naked grain. Robertson calls what follows a series of marvellous contrasts, the earthly and the risen differing in duration, value and power, and Wesley calls the word for sowing a beautiful one, the body being committed to the ground as seed. Clarke alone applies the earlier comparison otherwise, holding that the risen bodies, though all immortal, will differ in splendour according to the holiness of their souls, and reports the rabbinic scheme of seven degrees. Calvin refuses it, asking what connection the discourse would have if the apostle meant to distinguish degrees of future glory among the saints, and answering that he has followed one subject throughout.

The four contrasts are taken one by one. Barnes describes the sowing as a burial, hurried from the sight of friends and offensive as a mass turning to decay, with an ignominy attending it as under the curse, and the raising as a removal of that curse. Gill traces the dishonour further back, to a shameful original and a conception in sin. Clarke says the body is stripped of the glory it had as a machine fearfully and wonderfully made, and raised glorious because immortal and for ever redeemed from the empire of death. Wesley makes it shocking to those who loved it best, human nature in disgrace, then clothed with robes of light. Robertson locates the weakness in the victory of death and the power in this, that death can never conquer the new body.

The pair of adjectives is harder. Barnes says the first denotes what is endowed with animal life and breath. Clarke expands it into an anatomy of solids and fluids of different functions, of muscles, fibres, tendons, bones, arteries, veins and nerves, requiring continual support from food and therefore labour to provide it. Robertson admits the word is hard to translate and that natural, though as good as can be made, is not adequate, and warns that the risen body is not wholly spirit either. Ellicott finds in the analogies not only variety but adaptability, the body a plant has as seed suiting the condition of seed and the body it has when grown suiting the new one. Wesley says the present body is maintained by food and sleep and air like the bodies of brutes, the risen being of a more refined contexture and needing none of these.

The proof is drawn from the two Adams. Calvin says the apostle quotes Scripture lest the doctrine seem a new contrivance of his own, and that the Hebrew word there is taken in various senses. Barnes observes that only part of the verse is quoted, the words first and Adam being added to designate whom he meant. Ellicott reports the rabbinical explanation, that God breathed the breath of life into man and yet he became only a living soul, in whom the merely human faculties held sway. Clarke says the forms of expression are common among the Jews, who speak of Adam the first and Adam the last and assert two Adams, the heavenly and the earthly. Lightfoot asks where the second half is written, the first being plain, and answers that it is written throughout the whole sacred book, whence the Jews speak so many great things of the Spirit of Messiah. Robertson says Christ is the crown of humanity and has power to give us the new body, and Wesley that having life in himself he quickens whom he will.
46:
The order is insisted on. Robertson says the natural comes before the spiritual, and calls this the law of growth. Barnes finds the same rule everywhere, the imperfect succeeded by the perfect and the degraded by the glorious, so that there is a tendency towards perfection which God observes throughout. Gill notes that the spiritual body, though the more excellent, was not first. Ellicott adds this to what the analogies gave, so that there is not only a variety of bodies regulated by adaptability, but an ordered sequence in the variety. Calvin puts it as a necessity, that before we are restored in Christ we derive our origin from Adam, so that we need not wonder to begin with the lower. Clarke identifies the first with the body in which Adam was created and the second with that of the resurrection.

The two men are then described. Gill says the first was formed out of the earth, the word there signifying red earth, whence the name was given. Barnes calls him a mass of animated clay, of a nature low and corruptible, and says Christ is the second man as the second who sustained a relation to men affecting their destiny. Clarke says what is formed of earth must live after an earthly manner. Ellicott notes that the words the Lord are absent from the best manuscripts and that the preposition means originating from. Robertson grants that Christ had a human body but places the contrast between the first man in his natural body and the Second Man in his risen one, adding that the apostle saw him from heaven. Wesley explains why the symmetry is broken: it could not so well be said heavenly as earthy, since though man owes it to the earth that he is earthy, the Lord does not owe his glory to heaven, having made the heavens himself. Calvin reports that the Manichees perverted the verse to prove that Christ brought a body from heaven into the womb of the Virgin, and answers that they mistook what is spoken of here.

Chrysostom marks what kind of difference this is. The former, he says, was between the present life and that to come, but this one between the state before grace and after it; and the apostle states it with a view to the most excellent way of life, lest confidence in the resurrection make men neglectful of their practice.

The likeness follows the descent. Gill says the bodies of Adam's posterity are houses of clay, which rise out of the earth and return to it. Barnes and Clarke say the same, that all who derive their nature from him are frail and subject to death, while the state of the glorified will belong to all found fit for glory. Wesley distinguishes by principle rather than descent: the earthy continue without a higher principle, the heavenly receive a divine one. On the closing clause the text itself is disputed. Ellicott says the best manuscripts read let us bear rather than we shall bear, and that the words transport the thoughts to future glory while throwing light on present duty, the resurrection life being begun in us now. Robertson reports the same reading and yet resists it, suggesting it may be merely the failure of scribes to distinguish two similar vowels, since the apostle can hardly mean that our attaining the resurrection body depends on our own efforts. Calvin reports that some, taking the verse for an exhortation into which the apostle was led by digression, have changed the verb from future to hortative, and that some Greek copies read it so, but judges it unsuited to the argument. Gill takes the image borne to be not so much the sinful image on the soul as that of frailty and mortality on the body, and Wesley the other to be holiness and glory.
50:
Clarke calls the phrase a Hebrew periphrasis for man in his present infirmity, whose nature is not suited to that place, since he could not now endure an eternal weight of glory. Ellicott notes that the introducing formula is used for statements of profound significance, and that the reply no longer rests on analogy but comes as revelation. Barnes says it covers living and dead alike, an important change passing on both before they are fit for heaven. Calvin makes it the ground of all that went before, that bodies liable to corruption cannot inherit an incorruptible kingdom, so that there is no admission for us but by Christ's renewing us after his own image. Wesley says the flesh and blood we now wear cannot enter a kingdom wholly spiritual. Robertson draws the consequence that a change must come, and observes that in Christ's case it was wrought in less than three days, the body being even then in transition, since he ate and could be handled and yet passed through closed doors.

What follows is called a mystery. Gill says it is a secret reason could never have discovered, mentioned by no prophet or apostle but this one, and perhaps learned when he was caught up into the third heaven. Ellicott says a mystery is what has been concealed until now and is then made manifest, and refers the word forward rather than back. Calvin says it is so called because it had not been clearly unfolded before, and is said so to make them attentive; Clarke observes that the Jews had no distinct notions of it. Barnes says the third question of the chapter opens here, what becomes of those alive at the Lord's return. Henry states the substance, that not all the saints will die but all will be changed, living bodies altered no less than dead ones. Robertson cautions that the apostle claims no complete explanation, and that in saying we he groups all together without affirming that any then living would survive.

The speed is dwelt on. Barnes says the first word means an atom of time, a point that cannot be divided, and the second the least conceivable duration. Clarke renders it as soon as a man can wink, and says the raising of all the dead and the changing of all the living will be the work of a single moment. Robertson notes that the first word was the scientific term for what was thought indivisible, before electrons and protons, and that the second was used by the Greeks for the flapping of a wing, the buzz of a gnat and the twinkling of a star. Ellicott explains the trumpet as used to summon an assembly, the last concluding a series sounding at intervals in warning to the nations. Wesley exclaims at the omnipotence of it and asks whether the same power cannot now make us saints in a moment.

The last verse states the necessity as a clothing, Robertson and Barnes both giving the figure of putting on a garment. Ellicott adds that the risen body must suit not only the condition of the new life but its duration. Clarke says there must be a refinement by death or a change without it. Gill insists it is the selfsame body the saints now have, the apostle seeming to point with his finger at his own. Calvin says the passage distinctly proves that we shall rise in that same flesh we now bear, once delivered from corruption, since our nature as now corruptible is not admissible into the kingdom. Cyril of Jerusalem marks how pointedly the words are chosen: this body shall be raised, not remaining weak as now, but the very same body, which by putting on incorruption shall be fashioned anew, as iron blending with fire becomes fire, or rather as the Lord who raises us knows.
54:
The prophecy is traced. Barnes and Ellicott refer the first saying to the prophet, where it concerned the Jewish people. Clarke compares the Hebrew and the Greek, which reads that death having prevailed has swallowed up, while the later version of Theodotion agrees with the apostle. Robertson notes the change of voice and tense. Gill says the ancient Jews acknowledged the second saying to belong to the times of the Messiah, the Chaldee paraphrase interpreting it of the Word of God. Calvin calls the quotation a confirmation and not merely an amplification, since what the prophets foretold must be fulfilled.

The apostrophe is the turn of the chapter. Barnes calls it the beginning of the practical consequences, an exclamation any man with right feelings will make who looks on a world where death has reigned. Ellicott notes that in the prophet the terms stand in the other order, the second meaning the abode of departed spirits and not the place of torment, which has produced a variety of readings. Robertson says the apostle has put death for that word, which he never uses, and that the serpent has lost his poison fangs. Wesley distinguishes the terms, one relating to the soul and the other to the body, and says the invisible world is robbed of its spoils. Calvin leaves it uncertain whether the apostle speaks in his own person or still quotes. Cyril of Jerusalem turns it into a scene: death was struck with dismay on beholding a new visitant descend into Hades, unbound by the chains of that place, and he asks its porters what unwonted fear possessed them, since death fled and his flight betrayed his cowardice.

The sting and its strength are then explained. Gill says sin is the cause of death, which entered the world by it and is upheld in its empire through it. Barnes says the apostle personifies death as using sin for the envenomed instrument with which it inflicts the mortal agony. Clarke says death could not have entered the world if sin had not entered first, and that sin both introduced and armed him. Ellicott pictures death as a monster armed with a sting, and says that without sin it could not inflict pain, the strength of sin springing from its being a violation of God's law. Calvin puts it as a chain of causes: death has no dart but sin, since death proceeds from the anger of God and God is angry only with our sins, so that if sin is taken away death can no more harm us. Wesley adds that none can resist this sting by his own strength.

The thanksgiving and the charge close the chapter. Barnes says God alone is the author of the victory, having formed the plan, executed it in the gift of his Son and given it to us when we come to die. Clarke says what the law could not do, since law cannot pardon, the gospel has done, Christ having died to slay death and risen to bring mankind from under that empire. Ellicott observes that the future is so certain that it is made matter for present thanksgiving, and Calvin explains why sin and the law were named at all in a discourse on death, since Christ by conquering sin procured the victory. On the final exhortation Henry counts three charges, to be steadfast, unmovable and always abounding in the work of the Lord. Clarke derives the first word from a seat, bidding them confide in the doctrine as a man sits on one he knows solid. Wesley distinguishes the first two, steadfast in themselves and unmovable by others, and Calvin says the charge has more force than a simple conclusion, resting on the reward laid up with God. Robertson renders the imperatives as keep on becoming steadfast and unshaken, and remarks that the best answer to doubt is work.
